title: The Hollow Plan
author: Matthew Evans
summary: Matthew Evans argues that most school improvement plans are 'hollow' because they identify what leaders want to change without explaining why things are as they are or how the proposed change will actually make things better. The Ofsted self-evaluation process has been corrupted by deficit frameworks that essentially write improvement plans automatically -- priorities being whatever criteria are not yet ticked off on the inspection checklist. Evans identifies two critical types of explanation that hollow plans lack: a causal theory (why things are as they are) and a theory of change (how proposed actions will actually improve outcomes). Without these, improvement priorities are conjuring tricks. The article uses a punctuality problem as a worked example to show how weak causal theories lead to misguided interventions, and argues that brave headteachers must resist the temptation to let Ofsted frameworks do their thinking for them.
points: School improvement plans that name priorities without explaining the underlying causal theory risk being misguided and ineffective because they address symptoms rather than the mechanisms producing them.

The Ofsted self-evaluation process has turned 'knowing your school' into a deficit-model exercise where improvement plans almost write themselves -- priorities being whatever inspection criteria are not yet secure.

Two types of explanation are necessary for any genuine improvement plan: a causal theory (why things are as they are) and a theory of change (a plausible account of how proposed actions will produce improvement).

Improvement work on specific problems (e.g., student punctuality) is routinely misguided because leaders assume a single cause without speculating across the full range of possibilities, missing the real structural driver.

Without explanatory depth, school improvement plans are just words on a page: random rabbits pulled from a hat that consume institutional energy without generating the understanding needed to actually improve.
quotes: At this time of year, headteachers are asked to perform a conjuring trick - to pull a rabbit from a hat. Or rather a number of rabbits; the school improvement priorities for the coming year. In the hat are an almost infinite number of possibilities. Which ones will they pull out? What objects will be written into the school improvement plan for the coming year?

In the era of technocratic self-evaluation, school improvement priorities often arise as gaps between what is and what is expected, a deficit framing of the school, where attention is required in the areas where the school falls short of the idealised, abstract model of what a school should be.

Given the above, it is not surprising that many school improvement plans point to what leaders want to change without an explanation of why or how. They lack explanatory depth. This is a critical flaw as without a theoretical underpinning, the desired change is very unlikely to happen.

There are two types of explanation that are critical to school improvement planning. Firstly, we must seek to explain why things are as they are (a causal theory). Secondly, we must present a plausible explanation for how what we are proposing to do will make things better (a theory of change).
